title: Ambiguity Collapse by LLMs: A Taxonomy of Epistemic Risks

bias_targets.methodology: Conceptual analysis of how LLMs collapse ambiguous political concepts into singular perspectives, creating interpretive monocultures and hermeneutic capture. This is evaluated through real-world case studies, such as Grok 4 tracking specific political figures' views and the application of political bias rubrics in LLM-as-a-judge frameworks.

Theoretical evaluation of 'normative smuggling,' demonstrated through qualitative case studies of subjective tasks like hiring evaluations (defining a 'qualified' candidate) and model self-alignment. The paper examines how models impose hidden, singular value judgments instead of reflecting diverse user preferences.

Qualitative examination of how LLM-based religious tools (e.g., 'Fatwa Engines' or 'Digital Rabbis') collapse rich, pluralistic religious traditions into single, explicit operational definitions, leading to a breakdown of shared meaning.

Theoretical analysis of 'epistemic narrowing' and the 'loss of residuals,' illustrated by referencing systems that force genuinely indeterminate cases, such as gender-neutral names, into strict binary 'male' or 'female' labels.
